rationale:
TRIAGE: All candidates are direct-label matches (AAA) with broadly similar endpoint wording, so downstream comparison should focus on (a) what performance metric is being reported (PRS-only vs full model; AUC vs C-index vs OR/partial-r), (b) covariate packaging/cleanliness, (c) validation sample size and cohort independence, and (d) training scale/ancestry breadth.

Shortlist:
- PGS003973: Same Nat Genet meta-analysis family as PGS003972 but reports a very strong discrimination metric (C-index 0.882 with CI) and has a relatively clean/simple covariate set (Age, Age^2, Sex). This could be a top pick, but the metric type (C-index) and whether it reflects PRS-only vs a packaged model needs careful checking downstream.
- PGS001784: Very large genome-wide PRS (PRS-CS-auto; ~911k variants) from a multi-biobank cross-cohort effort; has an explicit PRS-only R2 (Nagelkerke R2 covariates regressed out = 0.014661) and a huge EUR validation N (350,767). Strong candidate on robustness/scale, but the full-model AUROC (0.868) is not directly comparable to PRS-only metrics and could mislead a single-shot picker.
- PGS003972: Sibling of PGS003973 (same publication, same method/variant count) but reports AUROC 0.69 with smaller validation N (6,940) and unknown covariates. Needs close comparison with PGS003973 because differences may be due to outcome definition, time-to-event vs case-control framing, covariate set, or evaluation design rather than true PRS quality.
- PGS002054: UKB-derived LDpred2 score with very large training N (391,124) and explicit PRS-only-like metric (partial-r 0.0144). Also includes multi-ancestry evaluation distribution. Even without AUC, it’s a plausible near-tie with PGS001784 on PRS-only signal magnitude and may be more comparable on “PGS-only” axis than candidates reporting only full-model AUC.

Watchlist:
- PGS003429: Recent Nat Commun score (shaPRS + LDpred2) with full-model AUROC 0.708 and R2 0.00547, but covariates are unknown and metrics appear packaged (full-model). Could look weaker than others due to reporting choices; still worth keeping as a plausible alternative because it is purpose-built in a screening/cost-effectiveness context and may have different endpoint framing.
- PGS000753: Very small P+T score (29 variants) with an OR=1.37 reported and mixed-ancestry evaluation distribution. It may underperform genome-wide PRS, but it can be deceptively attractive because OR is easy to interpret and may look “strong” without being directly comparable to AUC/R2; also could be more clinically portable due to low variant count. Needs careful apples-to-apples comparison rather than dismissal.

Overall, the main downstream risk is being misled by non-comparable performance reporting (full-model AUC/C-index vs PRS-only R2/partial-r vs OR) and by sibling-record differences within the same publication family (PGS003972 vs PGS003973). Uncertainty: High: performance metrics are heterogeneous and often not explicitly PRS-only; covariates are unknown for some records; and two candidates are siblings from the same study where evaluation design differences could dominate. Downstream PICK should explicitly normalize comparisons around PRS-only metrics when available and otherwise treat full-model discrimination metrics as non-comparable context rather than decisive evidence. PICK: All candidates are direct matches to the target trait (abdominal aortic aneurysm) by trait_reported/trait_efo, so the decision hinges on strength/clarity of PRS-specific evidence, validation robustness, and avoidance of potentially packaged (non-PRS-only) discrimination metrics.

PGS001784 is best-supported overall because it provides an explicit PRS-only performance metric (Nagelkerke R2 with covariates regressed out = 0.014661) alongside a very large European validation sample (n=350,767) and a modern genome-wide method (PRS-CS-auto) developed across multiple biobanks, which collectively supports robustness and reduces reliance on a single-cohort evaluation.

Runner-up PGS002054 is close on the “PRS-only-like” axis (partial-r = 0.0144) with very large UKB training (n=391,124) and multi-ancestry evaluation, but has a much smaller validation N (n=19,545) and less directly interpretable PRS-only reporting than PGS001784.

PGS003973 and PGS003972 (same Nat Genet study family) report strong discrimination metrics (C-index 0.882; AUROC 0.69), but these appear to be model-level discrimination with covariate inclusion varying/unclear (and covariates unknown for PGS003972), making them less cleanly comparable as standalone PRS evidence than PGS001784’s PRS-only R2. PGS003429 similarly reports full-model AUROC/R2 with unknown covariates. PGS000753 is a much smaller P+T score (29 variants) with an OR reported, which is not directly comparable and is less supported than the genome-wide scores given the available metadata. CRITIC: No visible contradiction with selecting PGS001784. All candidates are direct AAA matches by trait_reported/trait_efo and similar phenotype wording, so the differentiators are (i) whether performance is clearly PRS-only vs packaged with covariates, and (ii) validation robustness.

PGS001784 uniquely combines: (a) an explicit PRS-only metric (Nagelkerke R2 with covariates regressed out = 0.014661), (b) very large EUR validation N (350,767), and (c) a modern genome-wide method (PRS-CS-auto) with multi-biobank development context. The reported AUROC=0.868 is clearly a full-model metric (since PRS-only AUROC is null), so it should not be used as the main basis; however the pick rationale already correctly anchors on the PRS-only R2 and validation scale.

Alternatives do not visibly dominate on the same comparable axis: PGS002054 has a similar PRS-only-like metric (partial-r=0.0144) but much smaller validation N (19,545). PGS003973 reports a high C-index (0.882) but it is not labeled PRS-only and includes covariates (Age, Age^2, Sex), making it plausibly packaged/non-comparable to PRS-only metrics; thus it is not a clearly better-supported replacement given the visible metadata. PGS003972/PGS003429 similarly rely on discrimination metrics with unclear/unknown covariate packaging, and PGS000753 is a small-variant P+T score with only an OR reported.

Therefore keeping PGS001784 is defensible given the visible records and the guidance to prioritize clean PRS-only evidence when available.

TRIAGE: Plan for downstream comparison should center on three distinct “families” that could each win depending on what PICK prioritizes (endpoint fidelity vs ancestry match vs metric cleanliness).

- PGS002738 (Alcohol use disorder; PRS-CS; multi-ancestry GWAS, EUR eval): Directly aligned to target trait label (alcohol dependence/AUD), has an interpretable discrimination-style metric (OR top 10% vs rest = 1.96 with CI), and a large-ish EUR validation N (7,900). Potentially misleading aspects that warrant careful downstream scrutiny: covariates are “Unknown” (hard to judge leakage/packaging), record_count=4 suggests multiple performance entries that could differ by cohort/modeling choices, and the GWAS ancestry distribution sums >100% (likely overlapping sources), so transportability claims need cautious reading.

- PGS000201 (Problematic alcohol use; PRS-CS; UKB-trained; EUR eval): Very large variant count (~1.09M) and relatively clean/explicit covariate list (sex, age, PCs, array, site). Has a comparable PRS-only style metric (ΔR² vs covariates = 0.01192) and a decent validation N (7,599). This is a plausible near-tie with PGS002738 because it has clearer modeling/covariate documentation but a slightly more measurement/proxy-like endpoint (“DSM-5 criteria count, log-transformed” under “problematic alcohol use”) rather than the direct AUD label.

- PGS002739 (Alcohol use disorder; PRS-CSx gene-based; AFR eval): Key candidate because it is the only explicitly African American/Afro-Caribbean evaluation (N=6,315) and reports OR top 10% vs rest = 1.76 (CI provided). It could mislead a single-shot picker because the model is gene-based with only 858 features (not directly comparable to genome-wide SNP PRS in breadth), covariates are “Unknown,” and its ancestry match advantage only applies if downstream use cares about AFR evaluation specifically.

PGS000202 is best treated as watchlist: it is a sibling of PGS000201 from the same paper/method/phenotype, but has much smaller validation N (1,251) and weaker reported incremental signal (ΔR² 0.00456; β 0.043 with larger SE). It’s still plausible if downstream prioritizes the simpler covariate set (sex/age/PCs only) or if the performance entry is otherwise more comparable/clean in ways not visible here.

Downstream comparison should explicitly normalize across metric types (ΔR² vs OR top-decile), check whether reported effects are PRS-only vs packaged with covariates, and treat “Unknown” covariates (PGS002738/PGS002739) as an uncertainty factor rather than a veto. Uncertainty: Key uncertainties are (1) non-comparability of reported metrics across candidates (ΔR² vs OR top-decile; β scales differ), (2) missing covariate details for PGS002738/PGS002739 which could hide packaging/leakage or simply incomplete reporting, and (3) endpoint alignment nuances: “problematic alcohol use”/DSM-5 criteria count vs “alcohol use disorder” label may or may not map cleanly to the target trait intent. Also, PGS002738’s multi-ancestry GWAS proportions appear internally inconsistent (sum >100%), so ancestry/transportability interpretation should be handled cautiously downstream. PICK: PGS002738 is the most direct match to the target trait (trait_reported: Alcohol use disorder; trait_efo: alcohol dependence) and has reasonably interpretable, standalone PRS discrimination evidence (OR top 10% vs rest = 1.96 with CI) in a sizable European validation sample (n=7,900). Compared with the closest alternative, PGS000201, it has better endpoint-label alignment to alcohol dependence (PGS000201 is framed as “problematic alcohol use” with a DSM-5 criteria count phenotype) even though PGS000201 has cleaner/explicit covariate documentation and a comparable validation N. PGS002739 is also a direct endpoint match but is evaluated in African American/Afro-Caribbean samples and is gene-based with far fewer features, making it less generally comparable as the primary direct-match pick given the target trait is not ancestry-scoped here. PGS000202 is the weakest sibling (smaller validation N and weaker incremental signal). Confidence is medium because covariates are listed as Unknown for PGS002738 (raising uncertainty about packaging/leakage and comparability), and because metric types differ across candidates (OR vs ΔR²), limiting strict apples-to-apples performance comparison. CRITIC: No concrete contradiction found with keeping PGS002738 as best pick given the visible records. It is the most directly aligned to the target trait label (trait_efo: alcohol dependence; trait_reported: Alcohol use disorder) among the candidates, and it provides an interpretable PRS-only style association metric with uncertainty (OR top 10% vs rest = 1.96, CI 1.54–2.51) in a sizable EUR validation sample (n=7,900). The main visible weakness (covariates listed as Unknown; record_count=4 implying multiple performance entries not shown) is an uncertainty factor but not enough, on the visible evidence, to displace it.

Alternatives are not better-supported overall on visible fields: PGS000201 has cleaner covariate documentation and similar EUR validation N (7,599) but is a more measurement/proxy-framed construct (trait_reported: Problematic alcohol use; phenotype: DSM-5 criteria count) and uses a different metric type (ΔR² 0.01192), making it a plausible runner-up rather than a clear upgrade. PGS002739 is direct-endpoint but evaluated in AFR-only (n=6,315) and is gene-based with far fewer features (858), so it is less generally comparable as the primary pick when the target is not ancestry-scoped. PGS000202 is visibly weaker than PGS000201 (smaller validation N and lower ΔR²).

TRIAGE: All three candidates are directly aligned to the target EFO (alcoholic liver cirrhosis) but represent distinct study archetypes and could lead to different downstream choices, so they all deserve close comparison.

- PGS000704: Very large training/validation scale (UKB; validation n=135,300) and extremely high variant count (183k) via snpnet multi-PRS. Reported discrimination is a C-index/full-model 0.711 with covariates (age time-scale, sex, batch, PCs), which could mislead a single-shot picker because it is not clearly PRS-only performance and is packaged in a time-to-event model.

- PGS004913: Newer, explicitly focused on alcohol-associated cirrhosis among heavy drinkers; modest variant count (20) and moderate training/validation sizes (~3k each). Reports R²=0.029 and OR top vs bottom deciles 4.4. Could be a strong endpoint-fidelity candidate for the intended context, but its smaller scale and different metric family (R²/OR rather than AUC/C-index) makes it easy to under- or over-value without careful comparison.

- PGS001777: Very small variant count (3) with a focused “genetic risk score” style; validation n=1,390 and AUROC 0.671 plus a large tail-contrast OR (top 20% vs bottom 20% 6.18). This can mislead because extreme-quantile ORs can look impressive even when overall discrimination is modest and sample size is small; also phenotyping_reported notes “Cirrhosis (males)”, suggesting potential sex-stratified endpoint/validation context that needs checking downstream.

Given these complementary strengths/risks (scale vs endpoint specificity vs metric/packaging differences), none should be deprioritized at triage. Uncertainty: Key comparability gaps: (1) metrics are not harmonized (C-index/full-model vs AUROC vs R²/quantile OR), (2) PRS-only vs full-model performance is unclear/absent for all, (3) phenotype context differs (general population vs heavy drinkers; possible male-only phenotyping), and (4) covariate/packaging differences (time-to-event model vs unspecified covariates) could materially affect apparent performance. These uncertainties make near-ties plausible and justify keeping all candidates in the close-comparison set. PICK: All candidates are direct matches to the target trait (trait_efo = alcoholic liver cirrhosis / alcohol-associated liver cirrhosis). PGS004913 is best-supported as a standalone direct-endpoint PRS because it is explicitly designed for alcohol-associated liver cirrhosis with clear phenotype alignment (phenotyping_reported matches), uses a standard PRS construction approach (PRSice-2), and reports PRS-attributable performance summaries (R² and PRS decile OR) without being embedded in an evidently horizon-conditioned/time-to-event full model. PGS000704 has very large scale and variant coverage, but its reported discrimination is a full-model C-index from a time-to-event framework with covariates (age as time scale, sex, batch, PCs), making the incremental/PRS-only contribution unclear from the visible fields; this packaging reduces confidence for selecting it as the primary PGS despite strong sample size. PGS001777 is also directly aligned but is a very small 3-variant score with smaller validation (n=1,390) and a phenotype note suggesting sex-stratified context (“Cirrhosis (males)”), which makes it less generally supported than PGS004913 for the target trait as stated. CRITIC: No concrete visible contradiction with selecting PGS004913. All three candidates match the target EFO. PGS004913 has the cleanest endpoint/label alignment (trait_reported and phenotyping_reported both alcohol-associated liver cirrhosis) and reports PRS-attributable summaries (R²=0.029; OR top vs bottom deciles 4.4) without being explicitly embedded in a horizon-conditioned/time-to-event full model in the visible fields. PGS000704 is much larger and more polygenic, but the only visible discrimination is a full-model C-index 0.711 with covariates and time-to-event packaging (age as time scale), and PRS-only/incremental performance is not shown, making it less defensible as the primary standalone PRS on the visible evidence despite scale. PGS001777 is directly aligned but is a 3-variant score with small validation (n=1,390) and a phenotyping note suggesting a sex-stratified context (“Cirrhosis (males)”), reducing general support versus PGS004913. Given these tradeoffs, keeping PGS004913 as best with MEDIUM confidence is defensible.

TRIAGE: Plan for downstream comparison should explicitly cover three main “families” plus a legacy baseline, because each family has different ways to look strong on a quick read.

1) MVP diverse-population method-comparison set (HGG Adv 2024; PheCode 411.3): PGS005047–PGS005059.
- These are the most numerous and include several near-ties on the reported European validation C-index (~0.75–0.77). A single-shot picker could over-index on tiny metric differences or on OR vs C-index reporting.
- Strong candidates to compare closely: PGS005048 (highest reported C-index among these), plus the cluster of very close C-index scores (PGS005052, PGS005057, PGS005051, PGS005050, PGS005058, PGS005054, PGS005059). These are plausible near-ties where endpoint definition and evaluation packaging details (covariates, metric type, and whether the reported statistic is comparable across records) may matter more than the third-decimal performance.
- Watchlist within this family: PGS005047/PGS005049/PGS005055/PGS005053 because they show notably smaller reported effect sizes (ORs near ~1.04–1.12) despite similar-looking C-index values in some cases; this mismatch could reflect different scaling/contrast definitions or reporting choices that can mislead if not checked side-by-side.

2) UK Biobank sparse snpnet set (PLoS Genet 2021; multiple angina endpoints): PGS001260, PGS001261, PGS001262.
- These have explicit PRS-only AUROC (~0.58–0.59) and incremental/full-model metrics with covariates; a single-shot picker could mistakenly choose based on full-model AUROC (which is not comparable to PRS-only) or be misled by the “doctor diagnosed” vs “time-to-event” vs generic label differences.
- Shortlist all three because they are internally comparable (same paper/method family, similar training context) but differ in endpoint definition and validation N (notably larger for PGS001262), which could change which is the cleanest “angina pectoris” operationalization.

3) UK Biobank “risk-factor integrated” vs disease-only PRS (Commun Biol 2024): PGS004527 and PGS004457.
- These are easy to mis-pick because they report only an OR (no AUC/C-index) and have “Unknown” covariates; also one is explicitly a meta/integrated model (RFDiseasemetaPRS) which may not be a pure disease PRS.
- Shortlist both to force a careful downstream check of what is actually being scored (disease-only vs integrated) and whether the reported ORs are on comparable scales.

4) Legacy UKB multi-PRS snpnet (Nat Genet 2021): PGS000703.
- Watchlist as a baseline/contrast: it is directly labeled “Angina” and has a reported AUROC (~0.593) but appears to be a multi-PRS framework with only a full-model AUROC shown, which can be misleading if interpreted as PRS-only performance.

Overall, downstream PICK should do within-family comparisons first (MVP set; UKB snpnet set; Commun Biol pair), then cross-family reconciliation focusing on endpoint fidelity (PheCode vs ICD vs self/doctor report vs TTE), metric comparability (C-index vs AUROC vs OR; PRS-only vs full-model), and packaging/covariate clarity. Uncertainty: High density of near-ties in the MVP 2024 set with very similar C-index values makes it unclear which differences are substantive vs reporting noise. Several records mix metric types (C-index vs AUROC vs OR) and sometimes only provide full-model metrics or unclear covariate context, so apparent superiority from a single headline number may not hold under like-for-like comparison. PICK: All candidates are direct matches to angina pectoris (trait_efo=angina pectoris), but they fall into distinct study families with different metric/reporting completeness. The MVP method-comparison set (PGS005047–PGS005059) provides consistent endpoint labeling (PheCode 411.3), clear covariates (age, sex, 20 PCs), and comparable discrimination reporting (C-index) in a multi-ancestry evaluation framework; within this family, PGS005048 has the highest reported European validation C-index (0.7669) and a strong reported effect size (OR 1.487, 95% CI 1.41–1.56), making it the best-supported direct-match choice among near-tied siblings. UKB snpnet scores (PGS001260/61/62) report PRS-only AUROC (~0.58–0.59) but their headline full-model AUROCs are covariate-inflated and not directly comparable to the MVP C-index; they remain solid direct matches but are less compelling on the visible standalone PRS performance axis. The Commun Biol 2024 pair (PGS004457/PGS004527) report only ORs with unknown covariates and include an explicitly integrated/metaPRS variant, reducing interpretability as a standalone disease PGS versus the MVP set. Given the dense near-ties in the MVP set, confidence is medium and several sibling MVP models are close runner-ups. CRITIC: Proposed pick PGS005048 is defensible on the visible evidence. Within the large MVP HGG Adv 2024 family (PGS005047–PGS005059), the records are directly aligned to the target (trait_efo=angina pectoris; PheCode 411.3), share the same covariate set (age, sex, 20 PCs), and report the same discrimination metric type (C-index) for European validation, making within-family comparison coherent. PGS005048 has the highest reported European C-index among the MVP siblings shown (0.7668757), narrowly exceeding close alternatives like PGS005057 (0.7663666) and PGS005052 (0.7662454), so selecting it as best-in-family is reasonable given the near-tie. Its reported OR (1.487, 95% CI 1.41–1.56) is also consistent with being among the stronger-effect MVP siblings, whereas some watchlist MVP records show much smaller ORs despite similar C-index, supporting the triage caution but not contradicting the pick.

No concrete visible contradiction favors switching to the UKB snpnet set (PGS001260/PGS001261/PGS001262): although those have large training N and explicit PRS-only AUROC (~0.58–0.59), their much larger full-model AUROCs are covariate-inflated and not comparable to the MVP C-index; moreover, the PRS-only AUROC values are not obviously superior to the MVP family on a like-for-like axis (and are a different metric). The Commun Biol 2024 pair (PGS004457/PGS004527) provide only ORs with unknown covariates and include an explicitly integrated/metaPRS model, so they are less cleanly supported as standalone PGS choices than the MVP records with consistent covariate reporting and discrimination metrics. Overall, keeping PGS005048 with medium confidence is appropriate given the dense near-ties among MVP siblings and cross-family metric incomparability.

TRIAGE: Two clear study families need deliberate downstream comparison because they differ on endpoint framing, ancestry, and what the reported performance actually represents.

1) UKB/European snpnet siblings (PGS001267 vs PGS001268): both are direct trait matches, same publication, same sparse 10-variant structure, and both report PRS-only and full-model AUROC with CIs in European validation. They are near-ties on visible metrics, but differ in endpoint framing (standard case/control vs time-to-event). This is a classic place where a single-shot picker could over-index on slightly higher AUROC without checking whether the endpoint definition (TTE) is appropriate for the intended downstream use.

2) UKB/European portability paper scores (PGS002089, PGS001876): these have larger training N and (for PGS002089) far larger variant count, but only report partial correlation (partial-r) rather than AUROC/R², making apples-to-apples comparison against the snpnet AUROCs non-trivial. They deserve close comparison because they may be stronger as “pure PRS” models (and have explicit multi-ancestry evaluation context), yet the metric mismatch can mislead a picker into either dismissing them or overvaluing them.

3) Taiwanese/East Asian GWAS-derived set (PGS003420/3421/3422/3423/3424): all are direct trait matches with EAS-only evaluation and similar validation N, but they differ by method and reported full-model AUROC. The top three by reported AUROC (PGS003420, PGS003421, PGS003422) should be closely compared as plausible near-ties; however, the covariates are “Unknown” and the metric is full-model AUROC (not clearly PRS-only), which is exactly the kind of packaging/adjustment ambiguity that can inflate apparent performance and mislead a single-shot picker. Keeping multiple EAS candidates on the shortlist forces downstream review of whether the AUROC reflects PRS contribution vs covariate model.

Watchlist logic: PGS003423 and PGS003424 are same-family EAS alternatives with somewhat lower reported AUROC but still plausible if downstream checks reveal differences in PRS-only behavior, variant handling, or robustness. PGS001876 is a plausible alternative to PGS002089 within the portability paper (different method, fewer variants, slightly lower partial-r) and could win depending on downstream priorities (e.g., simplicity/overfitting concerns), but on visible evidence it is less compelling than PGS002089. Uncertainty: Key uncertainties that warrant downstream inspection: (a) comparability of AUROC across records when some are PRS-only vs full-model and others only provide partial-r; (b) whether the EAS records’ “full_model_auc” includes covariates that materially drive discrimination (covariates listed as Unknown); (c) whether the time-to-event endpoint in PGS001268 is aligned with the intended endpoint definition compared with the non-TTE PGS001267; (d) transportability trade-offs between EUR-trained UKB scores with multi-ancestry evaluation vs EAS-trained/EAS-evaluated Taiwanese scores with higher reported AUROC but smaller validation N and unclear covariate packaging. PICK: All candidates are direct matches to ankylosing spondylitis, but they differ in endpoint framing and how cleanly PRS performance is reported.

PGS001267 is best-supported overall because it is a direct case/control ankylosing spondylitis endpoint with clearly reported PRS-only and full-model discrimination (AUROC with CI) in a sizable European validation set, and with explicit covariates listed (age, sex, array, PCs). This makes its performance interpretation comparatively clean and comparable.

PGS001268 is a near-tie from the same study family with slightly higher reported AUROC, but it is explicitly a time-to-event (TTE) framing; without additional downstream context, the standard case/control definition in PGS001267 is the safer direct-match choice.

PGS002089 (and PGS001876) are also direct matches with larger training N and broader variant coverage, but only provide partial correlation (partial-r) rather than AUROC/R², making direct comparability to the snpnet records less clear on visible metadata.

The Taiwanese/East Asian set (PGS003420–PGS003424) reports higher full-model AUROC, but covariates are listed as Unknown and the metric is explicitly full-model (not PRS-only), increasing ambiguity about how much discrimination is attributable to the PRS itself; additionally, validation N is much smaller. Among them, PGS003420 is the strongest runner-up within that family. CRITIC: Proposed pick PGS001267 is defensible on visible metadata and there is no concrete contradiction requiring revision.

- Trait/endpoint alignment: PGS001267 is a direct ankylosing spondylitis case/control endpoint (phenotyping_reported: Ankylosing spondylitis). The closest sibling PGS001268 is explicitly time-to-event (TTE), which is a materially different endpoint framing; absent downstream intent to model incidence timing, preferring the non-TTE definition is reasonable.

- Metric cleanliness/comparability: PGS001267 reports both PRS-only AUROC (0.7265 with CI) and full-model AUROC (0.7433 with CI) with explicit covariates, enabling clearer interpretation of PRS contribution than candidates that only report partial-r (PGS002089/PGS001876) or only full-model AUROC with covariates listed as Unknown (PGS003420–PGS003424).

- Near-tie check: PGS001268 has slightly higher full-model AUROC (0.7488 vs 0.7433) and PRS-only AUROC (0.7346 vs 0.7265), but the difference is small and does not outweigh the endpoint-framing ambiguity (TTE) on visible evidence.

- Alternatives: PGS002089 has larger training N and many more variants but lacks AUROC/R², making it hard to claim it is better-supported than PGS001267 from the visible records alone. The EAS-only Taiwanese models show higher reported full-model AUROC (~0.788) but with Unknown covariates and much smaller validation N; the AUROC may reflect covariate packaging, so they are not better-supported overall given the current evidence.

Thus keeping PGS001267 as best_model_id with medium confidence is consistent with the records and the provided guidance.

TRIAGE: Primary close-compare set should center on the candidates that directly target the target trait endpoint (aortic stenosis) or very near measurement/proxy constructs explicitly tied to it in the record metadata.

- PGS005252 (aortic stenosis; incident cases; LDPred2; very large variant count; explicit C-index reported; large validation N; includes multiple clinical covariates in the reported model context) is a strong direct-endpoint candidate and likely anchor for downstream comparison.
- PGS005254 (aortic stenosis; incident cases; PRS-CS; HR with CI; simpler covariate set) is a plausible near-tie with PGS005252 because it is also direct-endpoint but differs in method family, training scale, and covariate packaging; it could win depending on how downstream PICK values endpoint purity vs reported discrimination context.
- PGS005255 (mean pressure gradient) and PGS005256 (peak aortic velocity) are measurement-like constructs with trait_efo explicitly including aortic stenosis/aortic measurement and are evaluated against incident aortic stenosis; these can mislead a single-shot picker because their labels are not the disease endpoint, yet they may capture closely related biology and come from the same publication family as PGS005254. They deserve head-to-head comparison with the direct AS scores rather than being ignored.

Secondary watchlist are the hypertrophic cardiomyopathy scores (PGS004911/PGS004910/PGS000739/PGS000778). They are phenotype-misaligned to the target trait but could look attractive on generic signals (recent PRS-CS models with large variant counts and decent AUROC; older genome-wide significant variant sets; some include substantial clinical covariate packaging). These are exactly the kind of candidates that could mislead a single-shot picker if judged on performance numbers alone without enforcing endpoint alignment; keep them available but not in the primary close-compare set for the target trait. Uncertainty: Within the aortic-stenosis publication families, several candidates are near-siblings (PGS005254/PGS005255/PGS005256) with similar variant counts and shared evaluation framing; without PRS-only metrics (and with differing covariate sets and endpoints), it is unclear whether the direct AS score or the measurement-derived scores will be preferable downstream. Also, PGS005252 reports a high C-index but in a context that includes multiple clinical covariates; comparability vs the other AS candidates may depend on whether downstream PICK prioritizes the genetic score’s standalone contribution vs the reported full-model context. PICK: Direct-match candidates for the target trait (aortic stenosis) are PGS005252 and PGS005254; PGS005255/PGS005256 are closely related measurement-labeled scores but still evaluated against incident aortic stenosis, making them near-direct but not as endpoint-faithful as the explicitly labeled disease scores. Among the direct aortic stenosis scores, PGS005252 is best supported in the visible metadata: it targets incident aortic stenosis cases, uses a modern genome-wide method (LDPred2) with broad variant coverage (~1.12M), has large development (n=47,691) and very large validation (n=446,895) samples, and reports discrimination (C-index 0.87) plus an effect size (HR 1.92). While the reported C-index appears to be in a covariate-adjusted context (multiple clinical covariates listed), the overall record still provides stronger and more complete support than PGS005254, which lacks reported discrimination metrics and has less complete training/cohort metadata in the record. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy scores (PGS000739/PGS000778/PGS004910/PGS004911) are not direct matches to aortic stenosis and are therefore not supportable as the best direct-match choice despite some having strong performance for their own phenotype. CRITIC: No visible contradiction found with keeping PGS005252 as best pick for target trait aortic stenosis.
